title: Evaluation Metrics — Regression & Ranking
summary: Learn how to score regression models beyond a single error number, and why recommenders and search systems need ranking metrics like NDCG and MAP instead.

slides.markdown:
Two metric families, one question: **how good are these numbers?** Regression metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE, R²) score how close a predicted value is to the true one. Ranking metrics (Precision@k, NDCG, MAP) score whether the right items land in the right order — the value itself barely matters.

Pick the wrong family and you optimize the wrong thing: a search model with great RMSE can still surface garbage at position 1.

slides.subTitle: MAE vs MSE vs RMSE
slides.markdown:
**MAE** averages `|error|` — every miss counts once, in the target's units. **MSE** averages `error²` — a miss of 10 contributes 100x more than a miss of 1. **RMSE** is `sqrt(MSE)` — back in the original units, but still quadratically punishes outliers.

Example: errors `[1,1,1,10]` → MAE = 3.25, RMSE ≈ 5.07 — the one bad prediction drags RMSE up far more. Pick MAE when outliers are noise to ignore; pick RMSE when a big miss is genuinely worse.

slides.subTitle: R² and its limits
slides.markdown:
**R²** (coefficient of determination) is the fraction of the target's variance your model explains: `1 - SS_res/SS_tot`. It feels intuitive — 0.85 sounds like "85% good" — but it's relative to the variance of *this* dataset, not an absolute error size.

Two traps: R² **never decreases** when you add more predictors, even useless ones (use adjusted R² instead), and on a bad model or unseen test data it can go **negative** — meaning your predictions are worse than just guessing the mean every time.

slides.subTitle: Why ranked output needs different metrics
slides.markdown:
Regression metrics score **how close a number is**. But a search engine, feed, or recommender doesn't need the exact relevance score right — it needs the **order** right. A model can have terrible RMSE on raw relevance scores and still put the best result first, which is all the user sees.

So ranking problems need metrics that only care about **position**: is the truly relevant item near the top, and are irrelevant items pushed down? That's what Precision@k, NDCG, and MAP measure — RMSE can't.

slides.subTitle: Precision@k and Recall@k
slides.markdown:
**Precision@k** = relevant items in your top k ÷ k — "of what I showed, how much was good?" **Recall@k** = relevant items in your top k ÷ total relevant items that exist — "of all the good stuff, how much did I surface?"

Example: 10 relevant docs exist; your top 5 results contain 3 of them. Precision@5 = 3/5 = 0.6. Recall@5 = 3/10 = 0.3. Search UIs (few slots, users rarely scroll) lean on precision@k; recall matters more when missing a match is costly, like legal discovery.

slides.subTitle: NDCG — rewarding the correct order
slides.markdown:
**NDCG** (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain) doesn't just count relevant items in the top k — it weights *where* they land. Each item's relevance is divided by `log2(position+1)`, so a hit at rank 1 counts far more than the same hit at rank 10 — that's the **discount**.

Dividing by the **ideal DCG** normalizes the score to 0–1, so queries with different numbers of relevant docs stay comparable. Two rankings with identical top-5 items can still score differently if one buries the best match lower.

slides.subTitle: MAP for ranked retrieval
slides.markdown:
**MAP** (Mean Average Precision) rewards getting relevant results high *and* consistently. For one query, compute precision@k at every rank where a relevant item appears, then average those — that's **Average Precision**. MAP is the mean of AP across all queries.

Unlike NDCG, MAP assumes relevance is binary rather than graded, and it rewards a system that keeps finding relevant items throughout the list, not just at the top. It's a standard metric for evaluating retrieval systems end to end.

slides.subTitle: Ranking metrics vs classification metrics
slides.markdown:
Same recommender, two lenses. **Classification metrics** (precision, recall, F1, AUC) treat each item independently. **Ranking metrics** (NDCG, MAP, Precision@k) score the whole ordered list at once.

| Question | Classification | Ranking |
|---|---|---|
| Unit scored | one item | a whole list |
| Order matters | no | yes |
| Typical use | spam / not-spam | search results, feeds |

A model can have great AUC per-item yet mediocre NDCG if it's right on average but sloppy about *which* item goes first.

slides.subTitle: Raw RMSE across different scales
slides.markdown:
A tempting shortcut: compare two models by their raw RMSE and declare the lower one better. That's only valid if both predict the **same target on the same scale**. RMSE = 500 predicting house prices (six figures) is excellent; RMSE = 500 predicting a person's age is nonsense.

Even the same target on different subsets breaks this — RMSE on luxury homes will dwarf RMSE on studio apartments regardless of model quality. Normalize first: use **RMSE / mean(target)** or **R²**, which is scale-free, before comparing across datasets or targets.
